title: Pre-market briefing — 2026-08-12
description_html:
I'll research the overnight narrative context before drafting the briefing.

Pre-Market Briefing — Wednesday, August 12, 2026

The Setup

Futures point to a firm open with the S&P and Nasdaq extending Tuesday's gains while the Dow lags, and volatility has collapsed overnight even as the single most important data point of the summer lands before the bell. The tape is broadly risk-on: growth and small-caps are bid, the VIX is sitting well below its 20-day average, and gold is spiking alongside — not instead of — a firmer dollar, an unusual combination worth watching rather than explaining away. Three things matter today, in order: first, the July CPI print at 8:30am ET, the swing factor for the rate-cut debate and the reason the curve has already rallied into the release; second, the AI-infrastructure earnings complex — Dell, Oracle, Arista, Micron, Super Micro — that is doing the heavy lifting for Nasdaq futures and setting up Applied Materials' print tomorrow as the next read-through; third, a cluster of consumer-discretionary and mega-cap communication-services names (Home Depot, Uber, Lululemon, Meta) that sold off hard in the prior session without a clean single catalyst, raising the question of whether this is rotation or noise.

Overnight Tape

Risk assets are firmer across the board pre-market. S&P futures are up +0.30% , Nasdaq 100 futures are leading at +0.80%, Russell 2000 futures are up +0.67%, while Dow futures are the outlier at -0.10% — a split that lines up with the sector story below: tech and small-cap strength against Dow-heavy softness. Asia was broadly strong: the Nikkei 225 ran +1.63%, helped mechanically by a weaker yen (dollar/yen +0.12%) that supports exporter earnings; Shanghai added +0.51%; the Hang Seng was roughly flat at -0.19%. Europe, which has already closed for the session, finished softer — Stoxx 600 -0.16%, DAX -0.23%, FTSE 100 -0.10% — a quiet fade rather than anything dramatic. The standout is volatility: the VIX is down -4.8% to 14.55, well under its 17.0 20-day average, with the curve in contango (VIX3M at 18.53). That's a notably calm vol posture heading into a high-importance CPI release — either genuine confidence in the disinflation trend, or complacency that gets tested at 8:30am. The dollar index is up +0.18% even as gold rallies +1.89% and silver +1.50%, a divergence that doesn't resolve into a single clean narrative and is worth flagging as such rather than forcing a story onto it.

Rates and the Fed

The Treasury curve rallied modestly into the CPI print, with yields lower across nearly every tenor and the front end leading: the 1-year fell -3 bps to 4.00%, 2-year and 3-year both fell -2 bps to 4.20% and 4.25%, and 10-year fell -2 bps to 4.68%. The move looks like positioning for a softer print or at least confirmation that disinflation is intact, though the magnitude is modest — this is a lean, not a conviction bet. The curve itself remains solidly positive: 2s10s at +48 bps and 3m10y at +81 bps, a long way from the inversions that defined prior cycles, and the shape has been reinforced by the deterioration in the labor data discussed below. The effective fed funds rate is steady at 3.63%, unchanged from the prior reading, and there's no FOMC meeting between now and the minutes from the July 28–29 meeting due August 19 at 2:00pm ET — those minutes are the next scheduled window into how divided the committee was on the cut path. Today's auction slate adds supply to watch alongside the data: a $42 billion 10-year note auction and a $72 billion 17-week bill auction both price today, with a $25 billion 30-year bond auction following tomorrow. A soft CPI print combined with weak demand at the 10-year auction would be a genuinely bullish rates combination; a hot CPI print into weak auction demand is the scenario that would hurt both bonds and equities simultaneously. The vol backdrop — cheap and in contango — suggests the market isn't currently pricing that tail heavily.

Macro

The backdrop into today's CPI print is unambiguously softer on growth and labor even as inflation has been cooling. The latest CPI reading stands at 3.3% year-over-year, down from a prior 3.5%, and core CPI is at 2.5%, down from 2.6% — both released today at 8:30am ET, comparing against those prior levels. Core PCE, the Fed's preferred gauge, was last at 3.3% versus a prior 3.4%, with the next reading due August 26. The labor picture is the more striking piece: nonfarm payrolls fell -23,000 against a prior +20,000, a genuine deterioration, even as the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2% — a combination that doesn't tell one clean story and likely reflects participation dynamics rather than labor-market strength. Initial jobless claims ticked up slightly to 199,000 from 198,000, with tomorrow's claims report the next incremental data point. Real GDP growth slowed to 1.5% QoQ SAAR from a prior 2.1%, reinforcing the deceleration theme. Collectively, this is a market pricing a Fed increasingly torn between still-present inflation and a visibly cooling economy — a dynamic one recent analysis characterized directly, noting the report has arrived at a critical juncture for financial markets given the mix of inflation and labor signals. Retail sales on August 14 is the next release that could meaningfully shift this narrative.

Ranked Developments

Movers

The overnight and prior-session mover list splits cleanly into a confirmed-catalyst AI/hardware complex and a consumer/mega-cap decline that lacks a single confirmed news driver. Cisco is the standout pre-market decliner at -4.1% to $118.84, but the company doesn't report earnings until after tonight's close — this move looks like de-risking or positioning ahead of the print rather than a reaction to confirmed news, and should be treated as such. The rest of the pre-market tape — Netflix +1.1%, Micron +1.0%, Deere +1.0%, Applied Materials +0.9% — is modest and consistent with a broad risk-on tone rather than idiosyncratic news, with Deere in particular not on today's earnings calendar (its print isn't until August 20). On the prior-session gainer side, Super Micro's +19.0% move on 3.3x average volume stands out as the cleanest signal of genuine news; Dell, Arista, and Oracle's moves also carry above-average or in-line volume consistent with earnings-driven repricing. On the loser side, Uber, Lululemon, Meta, Home Depot, and GM all fell 2.9%–4.0%, but several came on below-average volume — Meta at 0.9x, Home Depot at 0.8x, GM at just 0.5x — which argues against a single confirmed catalyst for each name individually; the more defensible explanation is the sector rotation visible in the data (consumer discretionary and communication services were the two weakest sectors), and any name-specific driver beyond that should be treated as unconfirmed.

The next two weeks are front-loaded with the events most likely to move rates and equities together. Today's CPI print is the most immediate repricing risk, followed closely by retail sales on August 14, which will speak directly to whether the consumer-discretionary weakness seen in the prior session is fundamental or technical. The FOMC minutes on August 19 are the next real window into the Fed's internal debate, and the run of retail earnings that week — Home Depot, Target, TJX, Lowe's, Walmart — will stress-test the consumer read from multiple angles simultaneously. Further out, Nvidia's report on August 26, alongside GDP and Personal Income/Core PCE the same day, is the single biggest event risk left in the month given Nvidia's weight in the AI-capex narrative that's currently driving sector leadership.

title: Pre-market briefing — 2026-08-13
description_html:
THE SETUP

Futures are pointing to a firmly higher open, with the S&P set to build on last night's record close and the Nasdaq leading. The tape is digesting a genuinely mixed prior session — broad index strength alongside brutal single-stock reactions in two of the most-watched tech names — while the rates market continues to price a softening labor backdrop against a Fed that hasn't moved. Vol is quiet, the dollar is soft, and the curve has bull-steepened into today's session. Three things matter most: first, whether the post-CPI, post-payrolls repricing in front-end yields extends or stalls, since that's the engine behind the equity melt-up; second, Applied Materials reports after tonight's close, and given how violently the market reacted to Cisco's beat-and-guide overnight, positioning into AMAT is unusually fraught; third, crude's sharp overnight slide on demand-outlook cuts is a genuine cross-asset signal worth watching beyond the energy complex alone.

OVERNIGHT TAPE

S&P 500 futures are up sharply, with Nasdaq 100 futures outperforming and the Dow and Russell lagging — a continuation of the mega-cap-tech-led tone from the prior close. Asia was mixed: the Nikkei extended its advance as semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related shares followed Wall Street higher , while Hang Seng and Shanghai both slipped modestly. Europe closed lower across the board ahead of the US open, a quiet fade rather than anything catalyst-driven. Vol is notably subdued — VIX sits well below its 20-day average, with the futures curve still in contango, signaling no near-term hedging stress even with two major tech names getting hit hard overnight. The dollar index is soft, extending its recent drift lower, with yen and yuan both firming slightly against it while sterling is marginally weaker.

RATES AND THE FED

The curve richened across the belly and long end, with every tenor from 6-month out to 30-year posting a lower yield on the day while bills barely moved. The 2s10s spread remains solidly positive and the 3m10y spread is even wider, both consistent with a curve that has fully normalized out of inversion and continues to steepen as the market prices a Fed that's done hiking and increasingly likely to ease. The move is being driven by the same two data points reshaping the whole macro debate this week: a softer-than-expected labor market and CPI that cooled further. Fed commentary around the edges is leaning toward validating the market's dovish read — additional cuts are anticipated through the remainder of 2026 by a growing share of the sell-side, though that view is not universal and hinges on whether the growth slowdown implied by the jobs data is confirmed or reverses.

The one complication for the long end is fiscal, not monetary. Yesterday's 30-year bond auction cleared at the highest interest rate in a quarter of a century , a reminder that even as cyclical data argues for lower yields, term premium and supply concerns are working in the opposite direction at the long end — which is part of why the 30-year yield fell by less on the day than the belly of the curve. With effective fed funds unchanged and no FOMC meeting until after the minutes release next week, this remains a data- and supply-driven rates market rather than one waiting on a specific Fed decision.

Initial claims at 209,000 versus a prior 200,000 add a little confirmation to the softening narrative without being alarming on their own. RANKED DEVELOPMENTS

record fourth-quarter 2026 results and strong AI-fueled guidance , yet the stock fell sharply after hours, even as investors digest the sharp rally and margin signals that had built into the print. This is a warning sign for positioning heading into Applied Materials tonight: strong fundamentals are not preventing air-pocket reactions when expectations and prior rallies have run ahead of the numbers. Read as neutral-to-cautionary for the AI-capex trade broadly — the fundamentals remain intact, but the market is now pricing perfection, and any incremental disappointment is being punished disproportionately. Watch AMAT's after-hours reaction tonight as the next data point.

This is bearish for semiconductor-equipment sentiment into the print and a read-through risk for the broader AI-capex complex if guidance disappoints tonight. Watch the after-hours reaction and any read-through to Micron, KLA, and Lam Research tomorrow.

OPEC also cut its demand forecast for 2026 and, separately, world oil demand is forecast to decline according to the IEA's latest report. This is a genuine growth-signal datapoint layered on top of the soft labor print — both are consistent with a slowing global demand backdrop, which is disinflationary and rate-cut-supportive but also a mild negative read on global growth. Bearish for energy-linked equities and breakevens, modestly supportive of the bond rally. Watch whether energy-sector price action decouples from the broader risk rally today.

gold pulls back from a two-month high as markets reassess the Fed rate outlook , alongside broader softness in silver. This looks like profit-taking after a strong run rather than a change in the medium-term thesis, but it's worth flagging as the metals complex has been one of the most crowded macro trades this year. Neutral-to-bearish near term for precious metals; watch real yields for the next directional cue.

Philip Morris is firmer in a defensive bid, while Abbott and Booking are both softer, though no specific catalyst stands out for either move — both look like continuation of prior-session drift rather than news-driven repricing.

In the prior session, Cisco was by far the most dramatic mover, falling on nearly triple average volume even after delivering record fourth-quarter 2026 results and strong AI-fueled guidance — a textbook sell-the-news reaction given how far the stock had run into the print. Arista and Applied Materials both fell alongside it as networking and equipment names de-rated together, while ConocoPhillips slipped with crude. On the gainer side, Intuit, Netflix, Palantir, Adobe, and Micron all posted strong single-day gains, with Intuit's move on above-average volume the most conviction-backed of the group; the others traded on lighter-than-average volume, suggesting more short-covering or momentum-chasing than fresh institutional conviction.

The most consequential item on the calendar is the FOMC minutes from the July 28-29 meeting, due next Wednesday, which the market will parse for confirmation or pushback on the dovish repricing now embedded in the front end of the curve. Retail earnings cluster heavily next week — Home Depot, Target, Lowe's, TJX, and then Walmart the following Wednesday — and collectively they're the best read the market gets on consumer health heading into year-end, particularly relevant given the growth slowdown implied by recent GDP and labor data. Treasury supply remains heavy throughout, with bill auctions continuing alongside a 20-year bond auction next Wednesday and a 29-year bond auction the day after — worth watching given how much attention this week's 30-year sale drew on pricing. Further out, Nvidia's report on August 26th is the single largest event risk for the AI-capex thesis broadly, with Analog Devices, Deere, Salesforce, Synopsys, and Intuit's next quarter also on the docket that week.

title: Pre-market briefing — 2026-08-21
description_html:
THE SETUP

Futures are pointing to a bounce after Thursday's broad risk-off session, with the S&P 500 futures <span></span>up <span></span>and Nasdaq 100 futures leading gains, but the move sits on top of a Treasury market that spent Thursday reversing a rally and pushing long yields higher into the close. The prior session's damage was real and broad — S&P 500 -0.87%, Nasdaq Composite -1.00%, Dow -1.32%, Russell 2000 -1.34% — with Walmart's post-earnings collapse doing most of the index-level damage. Vol is up but not screaming: VIX at 16.01 is +7.5% on the day but the curve remains in contango, meaning the options market isn't pricing sustained stress.

Three things matter today, in order. First, the long end of the curve — 30Y and 20Y yields pushed higher again as the market questions whether the Treasury's long-bond buyback plan is a durable fix or a short-term patch, and that skepticism is about to be tested by a heavy auction slate starting Monday. Second, Walmart's beat-but-cratered print is the cleanest read yet on the health of the U.S. consumer, and it landed one day after the market fully digested July's negative payrolls print. Third, positioning is already shifting toward next Wednesday's Nvidia earnings, the single most consequential print left in this cycle for AI capex sentiment and market breadth.

OVERNIGHT TAPE

Risk is bid globally into the U.S. open. All four major U.S. futures contracts are green, led by Nasdaq 100 futures and Russell 2000 futures, a small-cap-favoring tilt that reads as a partial unwind of Thursday's rate-driven selloff rather than a fresh growth narrative. Asia was mixed overnight — Hang Seng outperformed while the Nikkei slipped and Shanghai was flat — but Europe is broadly higher with the Stoxx 600, DAX and FTSE all in the green as their session runs concurrent with the pre-market. The dollar index is softer, with euro and sterling both firmer against it and the offshore yuan also stronger, a dollar-soft, risk-on FX complex consistent with the equity bid. VIX's +7.5% move despite green futures is the one dissonant note — it suggests dealers are still marking up downside protection after Thursday even as spot grinds higher, and with VIX3M at 19.06 the contango structure says the market is treating this as event-risk hedging (Nvidia, the auction calendar, Warsh) rather than a regime shift.

RATES AND THE FED

The move that actually matters happened in the long end. Thirty-year yields rose to 5.23% (+4 bps) and 20-year to 5.20% (+3 bps), extending a reversal that began when a bond rally fizzled on skepticism about the durability of the Treasury's debt-management fix. Note this curve snapshot is dated to Thursday's close (Aug 20) rather than a live pre-market print, so it captures the move that drove Thursday's equity selloff rather than anything fresher. The belly is also under pressure — 5Y +4 bps to 4.39%, 7Y +5 bps to 4.53%, 10Y +4 bps to 4.69% — while the front end is essentially anchored, with 6M and 2Y unchanged and 1Y actually down a basis point. That combination is unambiguous bear-steepening: the market isn't repricing near-term Fed policy, effective fed funds sits at 3.63% and unchanged from the prior reading, but it is demanding more term premium for duration. 2s10s at +50 bps and 3m10y at +82 bps both reflect that steepening dynamic.

The proximate driver is fiscal, not monetary: a rally in bonds fizzled out and stocks fell on bets the Treasury's plan to curb borrowing costs is just a short-term fix, with higher energy prices stoking worries about inflation . The Treasury Department's move to more than double repurchases of 10-, 20- and 30-year debt over the next few months was meant to compress long yields, and the fact that it didn't stick is itself the signal — the market is telling fiscal policymakers that supply and inflation expectations, not buyback mechanics, are setting the long end.

On the Fed side, Chairman Kevin Warsh remains a relatively unknown quantity to markets in terms of reaction function — he was confirmed in a historically divisive vote and has been in the chair only since mid-May. His scheduled keynote on August 28 is the next opportunity for the market to hear him frame policy in his own voice outside of FOMC statements, and given the ongoing bond-market unease about fiscal dominance and long-end supply, any comment on the Fed's relationship to Treasury issuance or debt monetization would move the long end sharply in either direction.

Markets are reading this as a genuine demand-side warning about the U.S. consumer, not a company-specific issue, and it's arriving in the same week as the negative July payrolls print — a coincidence the market is not treating as coincidental. This is bearish for consumer discretionary and staples (both sectors are the day's worst performers) and the read-through to next week's retail-adjacent data and holiday-season guidance from other retailers is the thing to watch.

$1.44 billion in forced short closures that amplified the initial catalyst into a 6%+ Bitcoin move — which means it's a positioning unwind rather than a new fundamental catalyst. That makes it a decent read on risk appetite for today's session but a poor guide to where crypto goes once the squeeze is exhausted; leveraged positioning like this tends to give back sharply once it's flushed.

MOVERS

Pre-market flow is quieter and more idiosyncratic than the prior session's earnings-driven moves. ConocoPhillips is the notable pre-market decliner, plausibly tracking today's -1.83% drop in WTI crude given its direct commodity linkage, a reversal from its prior-session gain that likely rode the opposite move in crude. BlackRock, Palo Alto Networks, Uber, and Lam Research are all modestly higher pre-market; none has an identifiable company-specific catalyst in available reporting, so these moves should be treated as unexplained and likely reflect the broader risk-on futures tone rather than idiosyncratic news. On the prior session, Walmart and Deere dominate for the reasons above. Intuitive Surgical's -5.8% decline, Capital One's -3.7% decline, RTX's -3.7% decline, and Ford's -3.5% decline all lack a clear catalyst in available reporting and should likewise be treated as unexplained moves rather than attributed to a specific driver. The Treasury auction slate running Monday through Thursday of next week is the first test of whether the market's long-end skepticism is durable or a one-session overreaction — soft cover ratios on the 5Y or 7Y would validate Thursday's move and extend the steepening. Nvidia's earnings on August 26 is the single highest-impact event on the calendar for equity breadth given its weight and the market's dependence on AI capex as a growth narrative; Broadcom's report on September 2 carries similar weight for the semiconductor complex more broadly. Chairman Warsh's keynote on August 28 is the wildcard — his public remarks to date have been limited, and any signal on the Fed's posture toward fiscal dominance or the long end would land directly on a bond market already primed to react.

title: Pre-market briefing — 2026-08-24
description_html:
THE SETUP

Futures are pointing to a soft open after a strong prior session — the S&P 500 closed at a record clip Friday, but the tape into today's open is giving a little of that back, led by a semiconductor complex under pressure and a bond market that keeps steepening. Gold at an all-time high, utilities getting hit, and chip stocks bleeding pre-market are three signals from three different corners of the market all pointing at the same underlying tension: rates, Fed credibility, and positioning ahead of Nvidia. Vol is not confirming the equity unease — the VIX is down and sitting comfortably below its 20-day average, which either means the pullback is shallow and well-contained, or that options markets haven't caught up yet. The three things that matter today, in order: first, Nvidia reports Wednesday after the close and the entire semiconductor tape is already trading defensively into it; second, the Treasury curve continues to steepen with long-end yields grinding higher into a week of heavy note supply; third, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's credibility with the bond market remains an open question after a July meeting that saw open hawkish dissent, with his next public test — a keynote on August 28 — now on the calendar.

OVERNIGHT TAPE

All four major US futures contracts are red, with the Nasdaq complex underperforming — NQ futures are down -0.57% versus a more modest -0.17% on the S&P and just -0.04% on the Dow, consistent with the tech/semiconductor-led nature of the pullback. Asia closed broadly lower, with the Hang Seng the weakest major index at -1.89%, the Nikkei off -0.74%, and Shanghai down -0.59% — a session that tracked Friday's late-day chip weakness and general risk paring into month-end. Europe is holding up better, trading modestly positive across the Stoxx 600 (+0.11%), DAX (+0.06%) and FTSE 100 (+0.20%), suggesting the risk-off impulse is US/Asia-tech specific rather than global. The dollar index is firmer (+0.18%), euro and sterling both softer against it, and dollar/yen up +0.15% — a classic mild risk-off FX complex. The VIX itself tells a more benign story: it's down -5.5% to 15.13, below its own 20-day average of 16.0, with the term structure in contango — the options market is not pricing meaningful near-term stress even as futures sit in the red, an ambiguity worth flagging rather than resolving.

The curve moved higher and steeper across nearly every tenor Friday. The short end is essentially anchored — 1-month bills unchanged at 3.80% — while the belly and long end backed up: 2-year +5 bps to 4.24%, 10-year +5 bps to 4.74%, 30-year +4 bps to 5.27%. That leaves 2s10s at +50 bps and 3m10y at +86 bps, both comfortably steep. This is a market pricing a Fed anchored at the front end by the current effective funds rate of 3.63% while long-end holders demand more term premium — a dynamic that has been building since Kevin Warsh took the oath of office as Fed chairman Kevin Warsh on Friday took the oath of office as chairman and a member of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System in May. The July FOMC meeting exposed a genuine split on the committee: while the majority of members of the Federal Open Market Committee agreed with holding rates steady in July, three dissented, arguing instead to hike rates to combat above-target inflation . That hawkish dissent, combined with a Fed chair who campaigned for cuts before taking the job, has left the bond market visibly skeptical — the bond market has doubts about the inflation fight even as the Fed signals resolve. That skepticism is arguably showing up directly in the long end and in gold. Today's calendar carries no Fed speakers, but Warsh's next public appearance — a keynote on August 28 — will be parsed closely for any shift in tone, and this week brings heavy bill and note supply (13-week and 26-week bills today, a 2-year note tomorrow) that will test whether the recent backup in yields is enough to draw demand.

That combination is exactly why the FOMC split matters — doves can point to payrolls and slowing growth, hawks can point to still-above-target core inflation, and Warsh has to referee it in public in four days.

Notably, even solid results haven't been rewarded lately: Applied Materials beat estimates and was sold anyway Applied Materials (AMAT) Beat Estimates and Investors Sold Anyway , a sign the bar for "good enough" has risen sharply. That raises the stakes for Nvidia specifically — expectations for continued outsized AI-driven growth are high, and the market's recent behavior suggests it will reward acceleration, not just a beat. Bullish for the print itself is speculative; bearish is the more crowded read into it. Watch: whether the pre-market chip weakness is simple de-risking ahead of the event or the start of a deeper unwind.

The pre-market tape is dominated by chip and memory names trading lower ahead of Nvidia's report, consistent with the broader semiconductor de-rating that's been building for weeks. On the prior session's leaderboard, Tesla, Lululemon, Chipotle, Target and Deere all posted gains north of 4%, several on volume well above average — Deere's 2.1x and Target's 1.5x average volume in particular point to a scheduled catalyst rather than drift, though the specific driver for each isn't confirmed in the data available here, and it would be a mistake to guess. On the loser side, the pattern is cleaner: Southern Company, Duke Energy and NextEra Energy — all utilities — were among the worst performers, which lines up directly with the sector-wide utilities decline of -2.28% and the backup in long-end yields that makes bond-proxy equities less attractive. Intel's decline fits the same semiconductor-complex weakness hitting Micron and the equipment names. Philip Morris's slide has no clear catalyst in the available data and should be treated as unexplained rather than attributed to a story that isn't there.

title: Pre-market briefing — 2026-08-26
description_html:
THE SETUP

Futures are pointing to a flat, slightly cautious open after yesterday's broad rally, with the S&P 500 — the benchmark index of 500 large U.S. companies — sitting essentially where it closed. Bond yields fell across the board overnight, and gold is climbing again, both signs that investors are leaning toward expectations of slower growth and eventually lower interest rates. Three things matter today, in order: first, Nvidia — the dominant maker of chips that power artificial intelligence data centers — reports earnings after the close, alongside Salesforce and Synopsys, in the single biggest data point the market gets all week. Second, the Treasury is selling $72 billion in short-term bills, a 1-year note and a $70 billion 5-year note today, a test of investor appetite for U.S. government debt that will help set the direction of borrowing costs into the weekend. Third, a divergence inside technology stocks — chip and hardware names strong, software names weak after Intuit's disappointing outlook — is worth watching as a signal of how selective this market has become.

OVERNIGHT TAPE

Overnight moves were modest and mixed. S&P 500 futures (contracts that let investors bet on where the index will open) are down slightly, Nasdaq 100 futures — which track the 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq, heavy in tech — are off a bit more, while Dow futures are marginally higher, and Russell 2000 futures, tracking smaller U.S. companies, are little changed. That's a pause, not a reversal, after Tuesday's session in which the Dow and S&P 500 rose and the Nasdaq climbed further . In Asia, every major index closed higher — Japan's Nikkei 225, Hong Kong's Hang Seng, and mainland China's Shanghai Composite all advanced, continuing a firm regional tone. Europe is mixed but calm: the Stoxx 600 (a broad basket of 600 European companies) and Germany's DAX are barely positive, while Britain's FTSE 100 is fractionally lower. The VIX — Wall Street's "fear gauge," which measures how much price swing options traders expect in the S&P 500 over the next month — fell to 15.45, a level that signals low anxiety. It sits below its own 3-month average of 18.21, a pattern called contango that simply means traders expect calmer conditions now than further out — often a sign of complacency rather than genuine calm. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of major currencies, ticked up slightly, while the dollar weakened against the Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan.

RATES AND THE FED

Treasury yields — the interest rate the government pays to borrow, which sets the floor for mortgage rates, car loans and corporate borrowing — fell across nearly every maturity as of yesterday's close. When yields fall, it means bond prices rose, which usually happens when investors get more cautious about growth or start betting the Federal Reserve will cut its own interest rate. The 2-year yield, which moves closely with what investors expect the Fed to do in the near term, dropped 7 basis points — a basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point, so this is a drop of seven-hundredths of one percent — to 4.17%. The 10-year yield, the benchmark that mortgage rates track most directly, fell 6 basis points to 4.64%. The gap between the 2-year and 10-year yields, known as the 2s10s spread and watched as a recession indicator, sits at +47 bps, meaning long-term rates still pay more than short-term ones — a normal, healthy shape, not the inverted one that has worried economists in recent years. Note this curve data is from Tuesday's close; today's fresh levels aren't in yet this early.

The driver is a cooling growth narrative: last month's surprisingly weak jobs report and slower economic growth have investors leaning toward the Fed easing policy further, even though the Fed's own overnight rate — the effective fed funds rate — held steady at 3.63%. Kevin Warsh, confirmed as Federal Reserve chair earlier this year in the most divisive Senate vote in Fed history , delivers keynote remarks on Friday, and that speech will be parsed closely for how he plans to balance still-elevated inflation against a softening labor market. Today's action lies in the Treasury's own borrowing: $72 billion in 17-week bills, a $28 billion 1-year note, and a $70 billion 5-year note all get sold today, with weak demand pushing yields up and strong demand pulling them down further — a real-time referendum on investor appetite for U.S. debt right into the Nvidia print tonight.

No major economic reports are scheduled for release today, so today's story is about digesting what's already out. Inflation is cooling gradually: consumer prices rose 3.3% from a year earlier, down from 3.5% the month before, and core CPI — which strips out volatile food and energy prices to show the underlying trend — eased to 2.5% from 2.6%. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, core PCE, slowed to 3.3% from 3.4%, still running well above where the Fed wants it, which is part of why a rate cut isn't a sure thing. The labor market sent a genuinely worrying signal: nonfarm payrolls fell by a seasonally adjusted 23,000 for the month, compared with a downwardly revised 20,000 for June — the first outright job losses in a while. Unemployment actually ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2%, a mixed signal that likely reflects fewer people counted as actively job-hunting rather than genuine strength. Jobless claims, a timelier weekly gauge of layoffs, eased to 206,000 from 212,000, suggesting no fresh wave of firings. Growth itself has slowed, with the economy expanding at a 1.5% annual pace last quarter, down from 2.1% — the combination of softer growth and firm-but-cooling inflation is exactly the tension Chair Warsh will have to address Friday.

RANKED DEVELOPMENTS

MOVERS

Intuit was pre-market's biggest mover by far, extending Tuesday's earnings-day decline into a second sharp leg down as investors continued digesting weak forward guidance. Two other software names, ServiceNow and Adobe, fell alongside it pre-market, a likely — though not confirmed — sympathy move given their similar subscription-software business models. Amgen, a biotechnology and drugmaker, and Uber, the ride-hailing and delivery company, both rose modestly pre-market on no single obvious catalyst evident in available information. In yesterday's regular session, the standout gainers were clustered around AI infrastructure: Super Micro Computer, a server maker for data centers, jumped on volume below its own average, while Cadence Design Systems and AMD, both tied to chip design and manufacturing, rallied on heavier-than-usual volume — a pattern consistent with investors positioning ahead of Nvidia's report tonight. Dell also gained; Merck's rise lacks a clear catalyst in available information. On the losing side, Target and Nike both fell on elevated volume amid broader softness in consumer-facing retail stocks, Lululemon and Palo Alto Networks — a cybersecurity software company — declined without an identifiable stock-specific catalyst, consistent with the same cautious mood weighing on discretionary and software names more broadly.
